title: Is Your Brain the Worst Place to Store Ideas? Why I Built a Second One
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
TLDR; I was forgetting the lessons from my own writing, so I built an automated “Second Brain” on my website. It uses a daily GitHub Action and the Gemini AI API to turn my old blog posts into a daily pop quiz, forcing me to actually remember my own thoughts through spaced repetition.

The Problem Statement: Losing My Own Lessons

I have this terrible habit of writing things down and immediately forgetting them.

I’ll have a profound realization about life, write a whole Medium article about it, feel incredibly enlightened, and then by the time I’m ordering Teh Ais at Q’Bistro the next day, it’s completely gone from my head.

I realized that if I actually wanted to grow, I couldn’t just keep dumping my thoughts into the void. I needed a system that fought back against my own forgetfulness.

The Science: Why We Forget

There’s actually a name for this. Psychologists call it the “Performance Paradox” of Cognitive Offloading.

Basically, the moment we write something down or put it in our phones, our brains take that as permission to hit ‘delete’. It’s why we don’t remember phone numbers anymore. The researchers behind the “Google Effect” paper call it Digital Amnesia. Our brains are great at generating ideas, but they are terrible hard drives.

The Solution: Hiring a Robot to Quiz Me

I decided to build a “Second Brain.” But I didn’t want a static Notion board that I’d just abandon after two weeks. I needed something aggressive. I needed spaced repetition.

Back in the 1880s, a guy named Hermann Ebbinghaus proved that we forget about 80% of what we learn within 24 hours unless we actively force ourselves to recall it. Re-reading doesn’t work; you have to be quizzed.

So I wrote a small script for my personal website.

Every single day, while I’m asleep, this script wakes up, scans the articles I’ve published, and uses AI to generate a trivia question based on my own writing. When I open my site in the morning, it quizzes me.

It’ll ask me something I wrote about Qada’ and Qadr three months ago. Sometimes, I get the answer wrong. Let me tell you, failing a pop quiz based on your own articles is a very weird, humbling experience. But it works. It forces me to actively recall the philosophies I claim to care about.

The Philosophy: Why Build in Public?

You don’t need to code an AI trivia bot to do this. A physical notebook or a simple digital garden works fine (I actually built a Gratitude Journal into my site too, just to force myself to pause and say Alhamdulillah). The tool doesn’t matter. The point is to stop treating your head like a filing cabinet.

But I highly recommend doing it in public.

There’s a culture of hoarding notes and keeping our “Second Brains” private. But as a Muslim, hoarding beneficial knowledge goes against the whole point of learning.

The Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) said:

“When a human being dies, all their deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, or a righteous child who prays for them.” (Sahih Muslim 1631)

By building my Second Brain on a public website, I’m not just fighting my own amnesia. I’m putting those lessons out there. If someone stumbles onto my site and plays the trivia game about navigating a quarter-life crisis, and it helps them? That’s beneficial knowledge.

The Result

Stop trusting your memory. Write it down, build a system to remind you, and share it. Because your brain is definitely going to drop it by tomorrow morning.

Want to see what this actually looks like?

You can play my AI-generated Trivia game (and try out the Gratitude Journal) live right now on my digital garden: frdspuzi.github.io.

(Fair warning: The AI pulls from my actual thoughts, so the questions might get surprisingly deep!)

title: What is Scrum?
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
AR/SR Section: Try to answer before going through notes

  1. What is the main purpose of breaking the process into smaller, iterative cycles called Sprints in Scrum?
    a) To increase the length of the project
    b) To allow for more flexibility and quicker adjustments
    c) To reduce the number of team members needed
  2. Which of the following is NOT one of the three key roles in Scrum?
    a) Product Owner
    b) Scrum Master
    c) Project Manager
    d) Developers
  3. What is the primary responsibility of the Product Owner?
    a) To write code and test the product
    b) To define the features needed for the product and prioritize the product backlog
    c) To facilitate daily meetings
  4. What does the Sprint Backlog represent?
    a) A list of all possible features for the product
    b) The team’s commitment for the Sprint duration
    c) A visual representation of the project’s timeline
  5. Which artifact helps visualize the progress of the Sprint and shows remaining work?
    a) Product Backlog
    b) Sprint Backlog
    c) Burndown Chart
  6. What is the purpose of the Daily Scrum (Daily Stand-up) meeting?
    a) To plan the entire project
    b) To discuss progress, plans, and any blockers
    c) To demonstrate completed work to stakeholders
  7. During which ceremony does the team demonstrate completed work to the Product Owner?
    a) Sprint Planning
    b) Daily Scrum
    c) Sprint Review
  8. What is the format of a User Story in the Product Backlog?
    a) As a [role], I need [feature], so that [reason]
    b) I want [feature] because [reason]
    c) [Feature] should be implemented by [date]
  9. What is the outcome of the Sprint Planning ceremony?
    a) A list of completed tasks
    b) A Sprint Backlog
    c) A Burndown Chart
  10. What is the main focus of the Sprint Review ceremony?
    a) To plan the next Sprint
    b) To reflect on the Sprint and discuss improvements
    c) To demonstrate completed work to the Product Owner

ans: [1] b, [2] c, [3] b, [4] b, [5] c, [6] b, [7] c, [8] a, [9] b, [10] c

What is Scrum?

An agile approach that breaks the process into smaller, iterative cycles called Sprints, allowing for more flexibility and quicker adjustments.

Each sprint consists of:
Plan -> Build -> Test -> Review

3 Roles

  1. Product Owner
    - defines the features needed for the product,
    - prioritizes the product backlog (a list of features and tasks).
  2. Scrum Master
    - responsible for protecting the team from distractions, helps resolves issues,
    - facilitates the Scrum process.
  3. Developers
    - develops, tests, other roles to build the project,
    - collaborates to complete tasks and delivers increments of the product.

3 Artifacts

artifacts are key information or documents that provide transparency and opportunities for inspection and adaptation throughout the development process. They help the Scrum team and stakeholders understand what is being built, what work remains, and how the project is progressing.

  1. Product Backlog
    - A prioritized list of user stories (features) that could be included in the product.
     — User Stories
     — — As a ______
     — — I need _____
     — — So that ______
  2. Sprint Backlog
    - a list of user stories selected for the current Sprint,
    - represents the team’s commitment for the Sprint duration.
  3. Burndown Chart
    - visualizes the progress of the Sprint,
    - shows remaining work and helps track if the team is on schedule.

3 Ceremonies

ceremonies (also known as events) are structured meetings that facilitate collaboration, transparency, and inspection and adaptation within the Scrum framework. These ceremonies help ensure that the team is aligned, focused, and continuously improving.

  1. Sprint Planning
    - the team, Product Owner, and Scrum Master discuss and select user stories for the Sprint.
    - results in a Sprint Backlog.
  2. Daily Scrum (Daily Stand-up)
    - a short daily meeting where the team discusses progress, plans, and any blockers.
  3. Sprint Review
    - the team demonstrates completed work to the Product Owner.
    - the team reflects on the Sprint and discusses improvements for future Sprints.

title: Ever Wondered Why We’re Here?
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
If you are;
- seeking for Purpose and Meaning, or
- curious About Islamic Beliefs, or
- A Young Adult Seeking Direction

This exploration of life’s purpose, as illustrated by the Quran and teachings of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), revolves around three primary roles: worshiping Allah, serving as stewards (khalifah) of the Earth, and preparing for the eternal Hereafter through a life of conscious choices and accountability.

1. Worship: Building a Deep Relationship with Allah

Allah’s words in the Quran clarify our foundational purpose:

“وما خلقت الجن والإنس إلا ليعبدون”
“I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.” (Quran 51:56)

Worship in Islam is much more than performing rituals; it is an invitation to recognize Allah’s sovereignty, express gratitude for His blessings, and develop mindfulness or taqwa that shapes our lives.

a) Recognizing Allah’s Sovereignty: Submission and Peace

To worship Allah is to acknowledge His supreme authority over all creation. The Quran reminds us:

“وإلهكم إله واحد لا إله إلا هو الرحمن الرحيم”
“And your god is one God. There is no deity [worthy of worship] except Him, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.” (Quran 2:163)

This recognition invites us to submit to Allah’s guidance, finding clarity and peace by aligning with His wisdom:

“وما كان لمؤمن ولا مؤمنة إذا قضى الله ورسوله أمرا أن يكون لهم الخيرة من أمرهم”
“It is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decreed a matter, that they should [thereafter] have any choice about their affair.” (Quran 33:36)

b) Gratitude: A Pathway to Fulfillment

Gratitude is the heart of worship, a reminder that everything we have is from Allah. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) modeled this beautifully, saying, “Shall I not be a grateful servant?” (Sahih Bukhari 1130).
Allah’s promise to the grateful is clear:

“لئن شكرتم لأزيدنكم”
“If you are grateful, I will surely increase you [in favor].” (Quran 14:7)

In a world where more is often desired, this reminder helps us find joy in the blessings we already have.

c) Taqwa: Becoming Our Best Selves

Worship fosters taqwa, an awareness of Allah’s presence that builds self-restraint and purifies our intentions. The Quran instructs us:

“يا أيها الناس اعبدوا ربكم الذي خلقكم والذين من قبلكم لعلكم تتقون”
“O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous.” (Quran 2:21)

Mindfulness in worship guides us away from wrongdoing and leads us to the best version of ourselves:

“إن الصلاة تنهى عن الفحشاء والمنكر”
“Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing…” (Quran 29:45)

2. Being Khalifah: Embracing Our Role as Caretakers

As Muslims, we’re not only individuals but also caretakers (khalifah) of Allah’s creation. This role brings a responsibility that goes beyond personal actions to preserving faith and fostering unity within the community:

“إني جاعل في الأرض خليفة”
“Indeed, I will make upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah).” (Quran 2:30)

a) Preserving Religion and Unity: A Collective Responsibility

While appointed leaders play a part, each of us shares in preserving the faith and maintaining unity. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) emphasized this, saying, “There will be no prophet after me; instead, there will be caliphs…” (Sahih Bukhari 3455).

  • Strength and Stability: Unity is a source of strength. “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.” (Quran 3:103). This collective unity supports the preservation of Islamic values and strengthens our community.
  • Protection for Future Generations: By preserving Islam’s teachings, we ensure that future generations inherit an unaltered, complete faith:
“اليوم أكملت لكم دينكم وأتممت عليكم نعمتي ورضيت لكم الإسلام دينا”
“This day I have perfected for you your religion and completed My favor upon you and have approved for you Islam as religion.” (Quran 5:3)
  • Avoiding Discord: The Prophet advised against divisive behavior, saying, “Do not hate each other, do not envy each other, and do not turn your backs on each other.” (Sahih Bukhari 6065)

As khalifah, we protect and uplift our faith, setting an environment where future generations can thrive.

3. Life as a Test of Faith and Conduct

Life is described as a test, where every action shapes our hereafter. Allah reminds us of this purpose, saying:

“الذي خلق الموت والحياة ليبلوكم أيكم أحسن عملا”
“He who created death and life to test you [as to] which of you is best in deed.” (Quran 67:2)

Our earthly life is temporary, but through it, we prepare for a lasting reality:

“وما الحياة الدنيا إلا لهو ولعب وإن الدار الآخرة لهي الحيوان لو كانوا يعلمون”
“And this worldly life is not but diversion and amusement. And indeed, the home of the Hereafter — that is the [eternal] life, if only they knew.” (Quran 29:64)

a) Free Will and Accountability

Allah grants us free will, but with it comes the weight of accountability:
“And stop them; indeed, they are to be questioned.” (Quran 37:24). Our actions shape who we become and impact our eternal outcome.

  • Character Development: Accountability encourages personal growth, pushing us to reflect and improve. “And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow…” (Quran 59:18)
  • Building a Meaningful Relationship with Allah: Accountability deepens our connection to Allah, who is “sufficient as an Accountant” (Quran 4:6), fostering sincerity and purpose in our actions.

b) Reward and Consequence

In Allah’s divine justice, every deed is accounted for, no matter how small:

“فمن يعمل مثقال ذرة خيرا يره. ومن يعمل مثقال ذرة شرا يره”
“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.” (Quran 99:7–8)

This system of reward and consequence assures us that no good effort is wasted, reinforcing fairness and motivating righteous living.

TLDR; In Islam, life is a journey rich with purpose and potential, calling us to worship, care for creation, and prepare for an eternal reality. Each of these roles brings us closer to Allah, offering fulfillment in ways that transcend material life.

Understanding and embracing these divine purposes helps us approach each day with clarity, compassion, and purpose, knowing our lives are part of a meaningful, eternal design. In Islam, life is seen as a purposeful journey. Muslims are called to:

  1. Worship Allah by recognizing His sovereignty, expressing gratitude, and developing taqwa (mindfulness).
  2. Serve as Khalifah (Caretakers) of the Earth, preserving faith, unity, and leadership within the community.
  3. Live as a Test of Faith and Conduct, where actions shape our eternal outcome, embracing accountability and striving for righteousness.

Our lives are a balance of devotion, responsibility, and preparation for the hereafter, as outlined in the Quran and Hadith.

Understanding and embracing these divine purposes helps us approach each day with clarity, compassion, and purpose, knowing our lives are part of a meaningful, eternal design. In Islam, life is seen as a purposeful journey. Muslims are called to:

  1. Worship Allah by recognizing His sovereignty, expressing gratitude, and developing taqwa (mindfulness).
  2. Serve as Khalifah (Caretakers) of the Earth, preserving faith, unity, and leadership within the community.
  3. Live as a Test of Faith and Conduct, where actions shape our eternal outcome, embracing accountability and striving for righteousness.

Our lives are a balance of devotion, responsibility, and preparation for the hereafter, as outlined in the Quran and Hadith.

title: Power Management States in the context of PCIe
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
TLDR; PCIe Power Management States is needed for the efficient use of energy, extending device longevity, and enhancing system performance in environments where power consumption is a significant concern.

PCIe power management states can be compared to different computer power modes. L0 is like a computer fully powered on and active, handling tasks without any power saving. L0s is similar to a computer screen turning off — less active but able to quickly resume full operation. L1.0 is akin to sleep mode, where the computer uses less power and can wake relatively quickly. L1.1 and L1.2 resemble deeper sleep or hibernation, where the computer shuts down more of its functions for greater energy savings, thus requiring more time to wake up. L2 is like the computer being completely shut down, minimizing power use and taking the longest to restart. This spectrum of states allows a PCIe device to efficiently manage power based on activity, saving energy while remaining responsive when needed.

STATES

1) Active State

  • L0: The device is fully operational and active, transmitting data.

2) Low Power States

  • L0s: A very light sleep state where the link can quickly “wake up” to resume activity. It’s designed for very short durations of idleness.

3) L1 State and Its Substates

  • L1.0: The first level of the L1 state, where the main link is more significantly powered down compared to L0s but can still wake relatively quickly.
  • L1.1: A deeper power-saving state within L1 where additional power components, specifically the electrical circuits of the main link, are powered down, leading to greater power savings but increased wake-up time.
  • L1.2: The deepest power-saving state within L1, where even more components are turned off, maximizing power savings at the cost of the longest delay in resuming activity.

4) Deeper Sleep States

  • L2: A state where the device is almost completely powered down. This state is used for the longest periods of inactivity and has the highest power savings and the longest wake-up time.

title: The Art of Qada’ and Qadr
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
TLDR; Qada’ is what happens in your life, while Qadr is Allah’s complete plan, already written. Your sincere Dua and actions can change your Qada’, but this change was always known to Allah and is part of His Qadr. So, take charge, make Dua, and strive for positive change, because Allah is always ready to respond and guide you. Remember, “Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.” (Surah Ar-Ra’d 13:11)

Qada’ refers to the actual occurrence of events in our lives. It represents the unfolding of events as they happen, shaped by our actions and decisions.

Qadr, on the other hand, is everything that Allah has planned and written for our lives, including all events, big or small. It encompasses Allah’s complete and eternal knowledge of everything that will ever happen.

The Relationship Between Qada’, Qadr, and Dua (Supplication)

Qada’ is something that can be influenced or altered by Dua (supplication) and our actions. For example, if we face a financial problem, we might decide to start a food business to solve it. Initially, the business might struggle, but through sincere dua (supplication) to Allah for help, the situation changes, and the business starts to thrive with many customers.

Allah encourages us to make Dua, as stated in the Qur’an:

وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ٱدْعُونِىٓ أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبَادَتِى سَيَدْخُلُونَ جَهَنَّمَ دَاخِرِينَ ٦٠
“And your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will respond to you.’” (Surah Ghafir 40:60)

Furthermore, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) emphasized the power of Dua:

Jubair bin Nufair narrated that Ubadah bin As-Samit narrated to them that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:
“There is not a Muslim upon the earth who calls upon Allah with any supplication, except that Allah grants it to him, or He turns away from him the like of it in evil; as long as he does not supplicate for something sinful, or the severing of the ties of kinship.” So a man from the people said: “What if we should increase (in it)?” He (ﷺ) said: “(With) Allah is more.”
Jamiat-Tirmidhi 3573 (Hasan)

How Dua Interacts with Qada’ and Qadr

While our action of making Dua changed the outcome, both this change and our decision to seek help through Dua are part of Qadr — Allah’s preordained knowledge and plan. Allah already knew that we would face this difficulty, make Dua, and that the business would eventually succeed. This means that while Qada’ can be altered by our actions and supplications, everything, including this change, is still encompassed within Allah’s perfect knowledge (Qadr) because He is Al-Alim (All-Knowing).

The Qur’an reminds us of this comprehensive knowledge of Allah:

مَآ أَصَابَ مِن مُّصِيبَةٍۢ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ إِلَّا فِى كِتَـٰبٍۢ مِّن قَبْلِ أَن نَّبْرَأَهَآ ۚ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرٌۭ ٢٢
“No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being — indeed that, for Allah, is easy.” (Surah Al-Hadid 57:22)

The Concept of Responsibility and Change

We are reminded that we have the ability and responsibility to make changes in our lives:

لَهُۥ مُعَقِّبَـٰتٌۭ مِّنۢ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِۦ يَحْفَظُونَهُۥ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ ۗ وَإِذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍۢ سُوٓءًۭا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥ ۚ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَالٍ ١١
“For him [i.e., each one] are successive [angels] before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allāh. Indeed, Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves.” (Surah Ar-Ra’d 13:11)

If you make a change in your own condition, you are altering the Qada’, but this has always been known to Allah, as it is already written in the Qadr. Therefore, anything can happen if Allah wills, but you are ultimately responsible for your own Qada’.

Because Allah’s will is absolute, nothing happens outside of His permission. However, He has granted us free will to make choices and take actions that impact our lives. This balance allows us to have an active role in influencing our destiny, while knowing that everything is within Allah’s knowledge and power.

Sources:
- Quran
- Mufti of Federal Territory’s Office

title: Top 20 Words to Understand the Quran: A Data Analysis using Python
author: Firdaus Puzi
description:
Problem Statement:

  1. What are some of the words that I can learn, with minimum effort, to get started and understand most of the Quran?
  2. Using the Paretto Principle, 80/20, where 80 is the result of 20 of our efforts. Do the top 20 words mentioned in the Quran amount to 80% of the Quran?
  3. Additional: Most repeated verses in the Quran?

Data Preparation

To use English translation or original Arabic text?

Arabic text due to its complexity. English translation may not be a direct translation. There are 12 million distinct Arabic words compared to 170,000 English words in the Oxford English Dictionary. Leading to an approximate 71:1 ratio of Arabic words to English

To use CSV or API?

Decided to go for API from Quran.com due to its credibility and availability of returning Arabic string in simple format without Tashkeel.

Tashkeel are small markings that you put above or below the letters to indicate how they should be pronounced, specifically which vowel sound to use. Think of them like the vowels in English that help you know how to say a word. Without these marks, reading Arabic can be tricky because the letters alone don’t always tell you how they should sound.

Although we are sacrificing precision, due to the existence of Arabic words with the same spelling, but different Tashkeel. The text analysed will be simpler and more uniform.

Call API and save in a pandas dataframe
import requests
import json

url = "https://api.quran.com/api/v4/quran/verses/uthmani_simple"

payload={}
headers = {
  'Accept': 'application/json'
}

response = requests.request("GET", url, headers=headers, data=payload)

# Load JSON data
data = json.loads(response.text)

# Pretty print JSON data with an indentation of 4 spaces
print(json.dumps(data, indent=4))
df = pd.DataFrame(data['verses'])
print(df)
Saved Dataframe

The GET method will return instances with columns of id, verse_key, and text_uthmani_simple. As we can see, it has 6236 rows, tallying with the amount of verses in the Quran.

Data Manipulation

Since we’d like to investigate the frequency of words in the Quran, we’d have to find a way to separate the verses by words.

Split Method
df.iloc[0]['text_uthmani_simple'].split()
Loop through whole column, include into new Dataframe
# Dictionary to store word counts
word_counts = {}

# Split sentences into words and count each word
for sentence in df['text_uthmani_simple']:
    words = sentence.split()
    for word in words:
        if word in word_counts:
            word_counts[word] += 1
        else:
            word_counts[word] = 1

# Create a New DataFrame
words_df = pd.DataFrame(list(word_counts.items()), columns=['Word', 'Count'])
print(words_df.sort_values('Count'))

The result will be returned, but isn’t as readable since Arabic words start from the right. It messes up with the formatting. Hence, we’ll move the Word column to the most right.

column_order = [col for col in words_df.columns if col != 'Word'] + ['Word']  # List comprehension to adjust order
words_df = words_df[column_order]

print(words_df)

The result returned has more readability. Now, we must sort it in descending order for data analysis.

Data Analysis

Let’s take a look at our findings when its sorted by descending order.

print(words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False).head(30))

Despite being able to see it sorted, we do not know their rankings. Let’s includde the indexing to show this.

sorted_words_df = words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sorted_words_df.index = sorted_words_df.index + 1

print(sorted_words_df)

Now that we can see the ranking, we’ll have to find the proportion and cumulative proportion to determine how much in terms of percentage, each words are in the Quran, starting from the most frequent. This is to see if the top 20 words make up 80% of the Quran.

words_df['Proportion'] = (words_df['Count'] / words_df['Count'].sum())*100
words_df = words_df.sort_values('Count', ascending=False)
words_df['Cumulative Proportion'] = words_df['Proportion'].cumsum()
sorted_words_df = words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sorted_words_df.index = sorted_words_df.index + 1
print(sorted_words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False))

Filter out to see only the top 20 words repeated in the Quran with its respective counts, proportion, cumulative proportion.

Conclusion

1. What are some of the words that I can learn, with minimum effort, to get started and understand most of the Quran?
  • من (min): from, of.
  • الله (Allah): Allah (God).
  • ان (an): that.
  • فى (fi): in, within.
  • ما (ma): what, which.
  • لا (la): no, not.
  • الذين (al-ladhīn): those who, the ones who.
  • الا (illa): except.
  • على (‘alā): upon, on.
  • ولا (walā): and not.
  • وما (wamā): and what.
  • الى (ilā): to, towards.
  • قال (qāl): he said.
  • لهم (lahum): To them.
  • ثم (thumma): Then.
  • لكم (lakum): For you.
  • ومن (wamin): and from.
  • كان (kāna): was, were.
  • به (bihi): with it.
  • وان (wa-an): and that.
2. Using the Paretto Principle, 80/20, where 80 is the result of 20 of our efforts. Do the top 20 words mentioned in the Quran amount to 80% of the Quran?

No, the top 20 words mentioned only accumulate to ~20.83% of the Quran. Despite that, to get started with Quranic Arabic, these are the words that should be mastered first.

3. Additional: Most repeated verses in the Quran?
print(df['text_uthmani_simple'].value_counts().head(10))
  1. فَبِأَيِّ آلَاءِ رَبِّكُمَا تُكَذِّبَانِ
    “Then which of the favors of your Lord will you deny?”
  2. وَيْلٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ لِلْمُكَذِّبِين
    “Woe that Day to the deniers.”
  3. فَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ وَأَطِيعُونِ
    “So fear Allah and obey me.”
  4. وَإِنَّ رَبَّكَ لَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الرَّحِيمُ
    “And indeed, your Lord, He is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.”
  5. حم
    “Ha, Meem.”
  6. وَيَقُولُونَ مَتَى هَذَا الْوَعْدُ إِن كُنتُمْ صَادِقِينَ
    “And they say, ‘When is this promise, if you should be truthful?’”
  7. إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً وَمَا كَانَ أَكْثَرُهُم مُّؤْمِنِينَ
    “Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not to believe.”
  8. الم
    “Alif, Lam, Meem.”
  9. وَمَا أَسْأَلُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ أَجْرٍ إِنْ أَجْرِيَ إِلَّا عَلَىٰ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ
    “And I ask of you for it no payment; my payment is only from the Lord of the worlds.”
  10. إِنِّي لَكُمْ رَسُولٌ أَمِينٌ
    “Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.”

words_df['Proportion'] = (words_df['Count'] / words_df['Count'].sum())*100
words_df = words_df.sort_values('Count', ascending=False)
words_df['Cumulative Proportion'] = words_df['Proportion'].cumsum()
sorted_words_df = words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sorted_words_df.index = sorted_words_df.index + 1
print(sorted_words_df.sort_values('Count',ascending=False))

Conclusion

1. What are some of the words that I can learn, with minimum effort, to get started and understand most of the Quran?
  • من (min): from, of.
  • الله (Allah): Allah (God).
  • ان (an): that.
  • فى (fi): in, within.
  • ما (ma): what, which.
  • لا (la): no, not.
  • الذين (al-ladhīn): those who, the ones who.
  • الا (illa): except.
  • على (‘alā): upon, on.
  • ولا (walā): and not.
  • وما (wamā): and what.
  • الى (ilā): to, towards.
  • قال (qāl): he said.
  • لهم (lahum): To them.
  • ثم (thumma): Then.
  • لكم (lakum): For you.
  • ومن (wamin): and from.
  • كان (kāna): was, were.
  • به (bihi): with it.
  • وان (wa-an): and that.
2. Using the Paretto Principle, 80/20, where 80 is the result of 20 of our efforts. Do the top 20 words mentioned in the Quran amount to 80% of the Quran?

No, the top 20 words mentioned only accumulate to ~20.83% of the Quran. Despite that, to get started with Quranic Arabic, these are the words that should be mastered first.
